```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(BayesMallows)
library(parallel)
library(loo)
library(matrixStats)
```

## Cluster analysis on rank data with the BayesMallows package

In this simulation, I use ranking data in which assessors were asked to rank their relative liking of six fruits: apples, bananas, dragon fruit, passion fruit, pomegranates and mangos Each fruit was given a rank from 1 (like the most) to 6 (like the least). The assessors were forced to prioritise, meaning that no two fruits could receive the same rank. Consequently, every assessor's set of ranks is a permutation of the numbers 1 to 6, so the sum, mean and standard variation are identical for every data row. 

This constraint also induced dependence between the variables. If apples are given rank 1, all other fruits must receive a higher rank, so the variables are negativel correlated by construction. The data can also not be interpreted in absolute terms: an assessor who ranks banans 6th may still like bananas a lot, but simply likes the other fruits even more. 

Given this data structure, latent class analysis (LCA) and latent profile analysis (LPA) are poor choices for clustering The ranks are not nominal categories, since they have a clear ordering. Nor are they continuous, since the steps between ranks cannot be assumed to be equidistant. Moreover, bith methods assume that the variables are independent within a cluster (local independece), which is violated here because ranks are strongly dependet by design. Mallow models, in contrast, are built for exactly this type of data: they model the full ranking as a permutation and cluster assessors by their distance to a cluster-specific latent consensus ranking.

This simulation is written from the perspective of an applied researcher in psychology. The Mallows model is well described elsewhere, but simulating data is a way to understand how the model behaves without having to fully decipher its algorithmic machinery. Because the true structure of simulated data is known, it is possible to test the BayesMallows package and check that behaves in predictable ways, that is, that it recovers what was put into the data. This is a useful step before applying the method to real data. I am sharing the simulation so that it can be useful to other applied researchers and analysts who are approaching the Mallows model for the first time.

Feedback on tweaks, improvements and errors are greatly appreciated: kristin.oster@su.se

### The true consensus rankings 

There are two clusters of consensus ranking. The **Lunchbox Pragmatists** prefer fruits that are easy to bring along and eat on the go, without a high risk of getting squashed. They also want fruits that taste good and give them energy. The **Foodfluencers** do not care about practicalities. For them, what matters is that the fruit looks good in photos. 



|Fruit | Cluster A - the lunhcbox pragmatics | Cluster B - the foodfluencer |
|:-----: | :----: | :----:|
|apple |1 | 5|
|banana |2 | 6|
|mango |3 | 4|
|passion fruit |4 | 2|
|pomegranates |5 | 3|
|dragon fruit |6 | 1|

In addition, there are individuals who do not share a consensus ranking. The rankings of these assessors are completely random. This group works as a noise component, to test how the algorithm handles assessors who do not belong to any cluster.

### Simulating a dataset

```{r}
fruit <- c("apple", "banana", "mango", "passion", "pomegr", "dragon")
CR_A <- c(1,2,3,4,5,6) #the rankorder of the fruits
CR_B <- c(5,6,4,2,3,1) 
p <- c(0.4, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10, 0.06, 0.04)

#sample data

data <- rbind(
  t(replicate(1000, match(fruit,sample(fruit, 6, prob = p)))),
  t(replicate(1000, match(fruit,sample(fruit[order(CR_B)], 6, prob = p)))), #cluster B
  t(replicate(1000,match(fruit,sample(fruit, 6))))
  )  |>
  as.data.frame()

names(data) <- fruit

#check the sampling

table(rowSums(data[fruit])) # 21 for each row
table(rowMeans(data[fruit])) # 3.5 for each row
colMeans(data[1:1000, fruit]) #means should increase in the order of CR_A 
colMeans(data[1001:2000, fruit]) #should follow the order of CR_B 
colMeans(data[2001:3000, fruit]) # random: all close to 3.5

```

## Fitting the model

Step 1 - exploring nr of clusters
```{r}
cl <- parallel::makeCluster(detectCores())
mdata <- setup_rank_data(rankings = as.matrix(data))

model1 <- compute_mallows_mixtures(n_clusters = 1:3, #The model has convergence problems with >2 clusters. And we only need to check that it doesn't suggest more than two
                                data= mdata,
                                model_options = set_model_options(metric = "spearman"),
                                compute_options = 
                                  set_compute_options(nmc = 11000, burnin = 1000,
                                                      rho_thinning = 10, include_wcd = TRUE), #rho thinning saving every 10th value
                                cl = cl)
stopCluster(cl)

assess_convergence(model1) #chain convergence for the different cluster models
assess_convergence(model1, parameter = "cluster_probs") #CHeck convergence for posterior distrubution of cluster asignment probabilities Note that the posterior probability of 1 cluster is 1
plot_elbow(model1) #Antyder 3 kluster. Efter 3 kluster så planar det ut. Inte jättetydligt men så verkar det vara

```


Step 2 - fit three models and compare with K-fold cross-validation
```{r}
rankings <- as.matrix(data)
N <- nrow(rankings)
n_items <- ncol(rankings)

card <- get_cardinalities(n_items, metric = "spearman")
logZ <- function(alpha) log(sum(card$value * exp(-alpha / n_items * card$distance))) #normalising constant from before: Z(α) as a sum over distances, weighted by how many permutations sit at each distance. It depends only on α, so it is built once and reused everywhere.

# Pointwise held-out elpd for new assessors, given a fit on other assessors
heldout_elpd <- function(fit, new_rankings, thin = 1) { #thin just to make the loop faster
  nmc  <- fit$compute_options$nmc
  keep <- seq(fit$compute_options$burnin + 1, nmc, by = thin)
  alpha_s <- fit$alpha_samples                    # K x nmc
  rho_s   <- fit$rho_samples                      # n_items x K x nmc
  K <- nrow(alpha_s)

  tau <- matrix(1, nrow = K, ncol = nmc)          # K = 1: weight is 1
  if (K > 1) { 
    cp <- fit$cluster_probs
    tau[cbind(as.integer(cp$cluster), cp$iteration)] <- cp$value
  } #Cluster weight matrix, one row per cluster, one column per iteration

  n_new <- nrow(new_rankings)
  loglik <- matrix(NA_real_, length(keep), n_new)
  for (i in seq_along(keep)) { 
    s <- keep[i] 
      #for each draw s, and cluster k:
    lp <- sapply(seq_len(K), function(k) {
      a <- alpha_s[k, s]
      d <- compute_rank_distance(new_rankings, rho_s[, k, s], metric = "spearman") 
        #compute the distance between held-out rankings to that cluster's consensus rho
      log(tau[k, s]) - a / n_items * d - logZ(a)
        #and turn it into a log probability
    })
    lp <- matrix(lp, nrow = n_new)                # keeps shape when n_new = 1
    loglik[i, ] <- rowLogSumExps(lp) #sums over clusters on the log scale, giving the mixture log-likelihood per assessor for this draw
  }
  # elpd_i = log of the posterior mean of the likelihood
  colLogSumExps(loglik) - log(length(keep)) #likelihood averaged over the posterior draws, i.e. log of the mean of exp(loglik) down each column. colLogSumExps computes the log of the sum stably, and subtracting log(length(keep)) turns the sum into a mean. The output is the elpd contribution of each held-out assessor.
}

#the K fold loop for one model
kfold_mallows <- function(n_cluster, folds, nmc = 5000, burnin = 1000) {
  elpd_i <- rep(NA_real_, N)
  for (f in sort(unique(folds))) {
    train <- rankings[folds != f, , drop = FALSE] #alla som ej tillhör aktuellt fold
    test  <- rankings[folds == f, , drop = FALSE]

    fit <- compute_mallows(
      data = setup_rank_data(rankings = train),
      model_options = set_model_options(n_cluster = n_cluster, metric = "spearman"),
      compute_options = set_compute_options(nmc = nmc, burnin = burnin)
    )
    elpd_i[folds == f] <- heldout_elpd(fit, test)
    message("n_cluster = ", n_cluster, ", fold ", f, " done")
  }
  elpd_i
}

# Run it for several models, with the same folds
set.seed(123)
V <- 10
folds <- sample(rep(seq_len(V), length.out = N))   # generate 10 folds, assigning each assessor a fold at random. The folds are made once and reused for every model. This matters: every model is then tested on the same held-out sets, so differences between models aren’t due to which assessors happened to be held out.

cluster_counts <- 1:3
elpd <- lapply(cluster_counts, kfold_mallows, folds = folds) #Saves the elpd for each assessor, under each model
names(elpd) <- paste0("K", cluster_counts)


#summarise and compare

summ <- function(x) c(elpd = sum(x), se = sqrt(N * var(x)))
t(sapply(elpd, summ)) #t is transpose...

# Paired comparison against the best model
best <- names(which.max(sapply(elpd, sum))) #find the best model (highest eldp)
comp <- sapply(elpd, function(x) {
  diff <- x - elpd[[best]]
  c(eldp = sum(x), elpd_diff = sum(diff), se_diff = sqrt(N * var(diff)))
})

round(t(comp), 2)

```
```{r}
K2 <- compute_mallows(
      data = mdata,
      model_options = set_model_options(n_cluster = 2, metric = "spearman"),
      compute_options = set_compute_options(nmc = 11000, burnin = 1000))





```
Posterior probabilities for alpha values and rho
```{r}
assess_convergence(K2) 
plot(K2, parameter = "alpha")
plot(K2, parameter = "rho", items = 1:6)
```


Below, you can see that all individuals are assigned a consensus ranking. But some should be 50/50

```{r}
plot(K2, parameter = "cluster_assignment") # the assessors are sorted according to their maximum a posteriori cluster estimate.
plot(K2, parameter = "cluster_probs") #posterior density of cluster probabilities
```

```{r}
cluster_assignments <- assign_cluster(K2, soft = TRUE) # Soft = TRUE ger alla kluster-sannolikheter. Om FALSE, så kodas de bara in e de kluster de har högst pp att tillhöra
tail(cluster_assignments,50)
```
Interestingly, the model is quite certain about the last individuals as well, although we know that they do not belong to any cluster.....




Here are the latent consensus ratings, identified by the model, along with the true consensus rankings

```{r}

CP <- compute_consensus(K2, type = "CP") 
CP$cumprob <- NULL


stats::reshape(CP, direction = "wide", idvar = "ranking",
                 timevar = "cluster", varying = list(as.character(unique(CP$cluster))))


```
